raw:
These hypotheses come from general knowledge of NAS-Bench-201. The literature section was empty, so no retrieved findings were used, and I have not tested any of them against benchmark data.

Three patterns drive them:
- **Filling an empty edge:** adding any op to an edge that is currently `none` gives a larger gain than replacing an existing op.
- **Removing a strong op:** removing a conv, or the direct 0→3 skip, hurts more than removing a weak op.
- **Redundancy:** a skip on edge 3 (0→3) bypasses the rest of the cell, so other edits matter less when it is present. When edge 3 is `none`, the remaining paths become limiting, so removals there hurt more.
